articles.title: Who is really in charge of design at Apple?
articles.summary:
The company’s design team technically reports to CEO Tim Cook, but hardware chief John Ternus — reportedly the leading candidate to replace Cook — is now the design group’s “executive sponsor” internally. In that role, Ternus “represents the design organization in executive team gatherings and manages the group’s leaders,” Bloomberg reports.

articles.title: Google Pixel 10A review: Just buy the 9A
articles.summary: Google’s new midrange Pixel 10A isn’t even a spec refresh — it’s a rerelease of the 9A.
articles.body: I’m not entirely sure why the Pixel 10A exists. Google hasn’t upgraded the chipset, cameras, or battery in the new phone, and the tweaks it’s made elsewhere are minimal at best. The flatter camera island is good, I guess! In one sense this isn’t a big problem: The Pixel 9A is an excellent device, and for the last year was easily the best phone you could buy for $500 in the US. The new 10A is available to buy now at that same great price ($499 for 128GB of storage or $100 more for 256GB), but with the 9A still on sale, and dropping in price, there’s one big question: Why not just buy the 9A — which is almost the same phone — for $50 less? [Product: Google Pixel 10A | When Google first showed me the 10A I struggled to get a good sense of what exactly had changed, so I pored over the spec sheets to lay out every hardware change Google has made, no matter how small. Here they are: * The 10A is 3g lighter than the 9A, and fractionally shorter and slimmer, resulting in a slightly thinner bezel around the screen * The cameras are entirely flush with the body, not just almost flush * The screen is protected by Gorilla Glass 7i, compared to Gorilla Glass 3 * The display is 300 nits brighter at peak brightness, and higher contrast * The 10A has 30W wired and 10W wireless charging, up from 23W wired and 7.5W wireless * The 10A supports Bluetooth 6.0, compared to 5.3 on the 9A * The 10A supports Satellite SOS * It comes in some new colors That’s not a whole lot, and none of these features feel individually like game-changers, except perhaps the introduction of Satellite SOS, which allows you to contact emergency services even when you’re outside of cell coverage. If that, or maybe the slightly faster charging, is enough to sway you to the 10A, great! I think you might be in the minority. [Image: [Image: [Image: The exterior updates are subtle, but welcome. Last year’s 9A dropped Google’s usual camera bar in favor of a smaller camera that just barely rose out of the phone’s back. In the 10A Google has pushed this design further, making the phone very slightly thicker so that the camera is now not only flush with the body, but ever-so-slightly recessed inside. It’s a welcome counterpoint to the bulging cameras on other phones with bigger ambitions. Those justify their designs with cutting-edge camera hardware, but since Google decided to instead stick with older, smaller sensors and focus its photography efforts on software, I applaud the decision to repay that with the least obtrusive camera design on any smartphone right now. The phone as a whole looks great, even if the design isn’t especially novel. It’s simple, sleek, and comfortable to hold in one hand. It’s slightly larger than the $799 Pixel 10, despite using a similar 6.3-inch display, but the 10A is noticeably lighter, which more than makes up for the extra size. My black model — sorry, obsidian — feels a little conservative, but the berry and lavender versions look fantastic if you want a pop of color. [Image: The 10A and 9A look exceedingly similar, but they aren’t quite identical. The 10A has the same 5,100mAh battery as the 9A, though Google claims the phone can last an extra 20 hours in its Extreme Battery Mode. Laurian Clemence, communications senior manager and head of product at Google, attributes that to “improvements in both software and hardware, including an updated modem,” though says Google has nothing to announce right now on whether the 9A would receive, or already has received, those same software improvements. Either way, this is a big enough battery to last one day, but not two, which is basically fine. The slightly faster charging speeds are welcome, though still slower than many Android alternatives — and Google didn’t extend the Pixel 10 line’s Qi2 magnets down to the 10A, which really would have felt like a worthwhile upgrade. The phone also runs on the same Tensor G4 chipset as last year’s 9A. It’s absolutely fast enough for all the day-to-day phone stuff, even if it falls short of the most powerful chipsets on the market. Google’s decision not to upgrade the chip a year on feels a little stingy, but it’s only really likely to cause headaches if you’re hoping for a powerhouse gaming phone (which this isn’t), or are planning to hold onto it for the duration of the seven years of OS updates, by which point the G4 will be nine years old and feeling a little long in the tooth. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: The cameras are the same between the phones too, which was inevitable in retrospect: A quirk of Google’s lineup means that the Pixel 10 has the same 48-megapixel main and 13-megapixel ultrawide cameras as the 9A, and so this phone gets them too. These cameras felt just about good enough in the 10, but for a $499 phone I can’t complain much. I’m a fan of Google’s fairly natural processing, especially at night, when it mostly resists the temptation to over-brighten everything. The sensors are small though, so you’ll run into limits fairly quickly in low light, with noisy details and blown-out lights, especially on the ultrawide. There aren’t many better cameras at this price however, and none in the US, where you’d need to spend at least a few hundred bucks more for a meaningful upgrade. [Image: Camera Coach’s advice is so basic that I’m not sure who it would help. The camera is also where you’ll find the whopping two software features found on the 10A but not the 9A: Camera Coach and Auto Best Take. Camera Coach is an AI feature that will give you step-by-step instructions on how to frame a photo, most of which boil down to “zoom in to focus on the subject.” It throws up an error message and refuses to work most of the time when I try it anyway. Auto Best Take is pretty much what it sounds like: an automatic version of the existing Best Take feature, which merges photos of groups to get the best expression from each person into the same shot. Neither is much of a reason to spend more on the 10A over the 9A, and in a press briefing Google wouldn’t confirm whether they would remain exclusive anyway, or simply roll out to the 9A in a future software update. [Image: I know I’m griping about how little’s changed, but let’s be fair: This phone looks pretty great. We’ve had a few exceedingly iterative phone updates recently: Samsung’s Galaxy S26 flagships feel like routine spec refreshes, Apple’s iPhone 17E mostly just adds MagSafe and more storage. But both those releases put the Pixel 10A to shame — at least they changed something. The funny thing is, the Pixel 10A is still the best midrange phone in the US right now, and one of the better options worldwide too, which is mostly an indictment of what the rest of the industry is doing at this price point. In six months’ time, when the Pixel 9A has sold out its remaining stock, the 10A will be the best way to spend $500 on a phone. But while last year’s phone is still around, Google’s biggest competitor is Google. Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge --- Agree to Continue: Google Pixel 10A Every smart device now requires you to agree to a series of terms and conditions before you can use it — contracts that no one actually reads. It’s impossible for us to read and analyze every single one of these agreements. But we started counting exactly how many times you have to hit “agree” to use devices when we review them since these are agreements most people don’t read and definitely can’t negotiate. To use the Pixel 10A, you must agree to: * Google Terms of Service * Google Play Terms of Service * Google Privacy Policy (included in ToS) * Install apps and updates: “You agree this device may also automatically download and install updates and apps from Google, your carrier, and your device’s manufacturer, possibly using cellular data.” There’s also a variety of optional agreements, including: * Provide anonymous location data for Google’s services * “Allow apps and services to scan for Wi-Fi networks and nearby devices at any time, even when Wi-Fi or Bluetooth is off.” * Allow phone number verification * Send usage and diagnostic data to Google * Google Gemini Apps Privacy Notice if you opt in to using Gemini Assistant Other features, like Google Wallet, may require additional agreements. Final tally: four mandatory agreements and at least five optional agreements. --- Update, March 18th: Added comment from Google on the battery optimizations and the ‘Agree to Continue’ box.

articles.title: Amazon’s colorful and sturdy new Kindles
articles.summary: Plus: OpenAI’s Dots, the remastered Witcher 3, Bose’s new wired earbuds, and more.
articles.body: Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 146, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. (If you’re new here, welcome, it’s October already?, and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage.) This week, I’m wishing I could do Walmart potato drone delivery in Portland, watching Mike Tomlin explain his incredible Minecraft city, pondering if the Gears of War pizza cutter is awesome or terrible, exploring Craig Mod’s walks, nodding along with MKBHD’s video about YouTube’s A/B video testing feature, hoping that more concerts ban phones, and celebrating soup season. It’s here! Programming note: David is back next week! It’s been a blast writing Installer again, and thanks to everyone for reading and for your recommendations. For now, I also have for you Amazon’s new Kindles, OpenAI’s Dots, the remastered Witcher 3, and more. (As always, the best part of Installer is your ideas and tips. What apps are you into right now? What are your favorite things you’ve watched / seen / zoned out to recently? Tell me everything: installer@theverge.com. And if you know someone else who might enjoy Installer, forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here.) The Drop * Amazon’s new Kindles. Amazon might have crushed it with the Kindle updates this year. The new base e-readers look like they’ll be a nice upgrade from previous generations, with flush front screens, an option for an aluminum back, and some nice new colors. The new Paperwhite and Colorsoft Signature Editions are compatible with a case with page turn buttons. And now there’s a “Kindle Click” remote to let you turn pages and adjust brightness. My years-old Paperwhite is still trucking along just fine, but if it suddenly broke, these would be really tempting options. * OpenAI’s Dots. OpenAI’s Muse-like AI agent is here, though the company is pitching it more as something to help you with work than an all-encompassing assistant for your personal life. (That’s probably coming later.) The Dots are also adorable, though I think I’d give the Muse mascots the edge in cuteness. * The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered. Eleven years after its initial launch, The Witcher 3 is getting yet another big update. This free update for existing owners adds a lot of features and tweaks, including visual improvements, changes to skills, a new accessibility section in settings, cross-platform mod support, and more. The game is also now on Switch 2. Might be time for me to finally dive in. * Bose’s Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds. These $99 USB-C wired earbuds have noise cancellation and an in-line remote for adjusting volume with a built-in microphone for calls, and they come in three colors. As a huge fan of Apple’s wired EarPods, these could be a great option that’s a step above those in quality. * Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve. Bandai Namco’s latest entry in its fighter-pilot franchise sounds like a thrilling experience with a campaign filled with optimism, and it’s become one of the best-reviewed games of the year. Seems like a soaring success. * Keurig’s Alta. The new Keurig coffee machine can make you a cup of joe with compostable pucks instead of the recyclable pods. Plus, it can also make espresso and looks super fancy. It’s not cheap at $499.99. But it’s tough to beat the convenience of a Keurig — I learned firsthand when my toddler was a newborn — so this could be a good option if you want to lead a Keurig life with more Earth-friendly pods. * HP’s OmniBook 5 14. This HP laptop is thin and light, has 8GB of RAM, comes in good colors, and starts at $699.99, making it extremely MacBook Neo-adjacent. If you want the Neo ethos paired with Windows, this might be a solid option. * Ikea’s Förlig lamp. This LED Ikea lamp lets you swap between 10 different colors, can be used from the floor or on a wall, and looks kind of like a lightsaber. Super fun. Screen share Today I’m featuring Scott Stein, CNET’s editor at large. I’ve been a huge admirer of Stein’s work, especially his excellent coverage of wearables and VR, for years, and I had the great fortune of finally meeting him in person at Snap and Meta’s events last month. I asked Scott to share his homescreen and the apps and things he cares about. Here it is, plus some info on the apps he uses and why: [Image: The phone: I use an iPhone 16 Pro Max right now. The apps: So I randomize my Home Screen apps. Madness? Maybe. I started doing it for fun by adding suggested Siri app widgets a few years ago. I add two of the widgets, 8 apps each, and then the bottom 8 are fixed ones plus the four on my dock. My fixed ones are: Google Calendar, Photos, Notes, Camera, Music, Gmail, GMaps, Bluesky, Phone, Messages, Mail, Safari. My core go-tos. But the others are a contextual-slash-frequency-based mix of things I might be using (or not). The locations shift. In some ways it’s like Home Screen gaslighting… but it’s also a living Black Mirror life, and often it’s actually helpful. Today there’s the United app since I’m flying, Uber, Siri, Voice Memos, Signal, GChat, YouTube, Asana, Yahoo Sports… mostly pretty useful. The wallpaper: My background’s also randomized. I pull from family and trip photos so I can see my kids (and other odd moments) when I’m out and about. It comforts me. I also asked Scott to share a few things he’s into right now. Here’s what he sent back: The apps: * I have had an ongoing magic hobby since I was a kid. I’m reading The Intuitive Magician: Mastering Magic Through Improvisation, by Justin Higham. Kind of technical but it’s an exploration of where practice and fluid improvising meet, which feels holistic for other things. * Also reading Stephen King and Peter Straub’s Black House, after reading The Talisman. I loved the Dark Tower books and the new Talisman trilogy end is coming soon which apparently blends them all together. * I’ve also been semi obsessed with runes lately, part of my interest in portable trinkets and talismans, and how readings can feel like a form of meditation. * Still playing Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave, and carving out time ahead for Panic Playdate’s third season. I love that little handheld. Crowdsourced Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week. For even more great recommendations, check out the replies to this post on The Verge. “Arc Raiders (Expedition done and 2.0 coming in a week!) and Control Resonant. East of Eden.” — ProtoPhil “I just started Widow’s Bay last night. Currently reading The Velvet Rage. Listening to the new Orville Peck album, Madonna, Adele, Amy Winehouse. Playing Stardew Valley. — antwhat “Started watching American Horror Story: 13 and the first three episodes were pretty interesting! Love seeing the old characters’ reunion.” — alee “I’m watching Star Trek: Voyager again! Light, serious, funny and introspective, a great watch in a time where the AI news has been a serious of scary headlines.” — BlubberBacon “I’ve got a stack of spooky season reading that I can’t wait to dig into: The Nudge by Joseph Fink, Breakable Things and The Salt Grows Heavy by Cassandra Khaw, and The King in Yellow by Robert Chambers (Cthulhu’s grandpappy).” — Barbarian Librarian “I’m playing Antivirus Survivors 2003 Professional because I’m apparently an ‘unc’ gamer.” — bubble_boy “Two separate reading recommendations: Andrew Sacher’s Emo Revival and Tress of the Emerald Sea by Brandon Sanderson. Loved them both.” — securingsincity “The latest episode of South Park America was brilliant!” — verge_user_BlorpBlorp Signing off Remember my minimal homescreen I showed off in my first issue I wrote back in August? I have to confess: It became a mess of apps during my travels this month. Multiple airline apps, an expense reporting app, Notes, Voice Memos, Uber, and more — it gave me hives. Fortunately, I’ve finally gotten around to cleaning things up, and the screen is back down to just the Messages app once again. Calm restored. Well, until my next trip. See you around!

articles.title: The rise, fall, and rise of portable MP3 players
articles.summary: ﻿Apple perfected the media player with the iPod, then abandoned it.
articles.body: This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the collapse and the resurgence of the portable media player, follow Terrence O’Brien. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here. How it started We are spoiled for choice, musically. Most of us walk around with access to hundreds of millions of songs in our pockets. But it wasn’t until 1998 that portable digital music was even a thing. Before that we lugged booklets full of CDs on the bus or stashed a handful of cassettes in our backpacks. With the advent of the MP3 player in the 2000s we were soon able to carry massive libraries of music everywhere we went — over 1,000 albums’ worth depending on the file format and the size of your MP3 player. The MPMan F10 is generally considered to be the first commercial MP3 player. It was roughly the size of a deck of cards and looked like an oversized pager. It launched in Asia in March of 1998, but it barely made a blip on anyone’s radar. It was the Diamond Rio PMP300 that broke through in the West a few months later, in September of 1998. It was slightly larger, and its design more closely resembles what we envision when we think of a media player (namely the iPod). But even then, it drew more attention because the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) sued Diamond Multimedia in an attempt to stop the spread of MP3s. The F10 and the PMP300 were, unsurprisingly, primitive by today’s standards, shipping with just 32MB — yes, that’s megabytes — of storage. That tiny amount of built-in memory only allowed for around 12 songs to be stored on them. They held less audio than a CD and generally sounded worse. But it wasn’t that big of a limitation, in comparison to the nightmare that was the UI on their tiny monochrome LCDs. Plus, you could expand storage on both using SmartMedia cards if you really needed to. Eventually, some companies addressed the storage issue by swapping flash storage, which was still relatively limited at the time, for traditional spinning-disc hard drives. The Creative Nomad Jukebox, for instance, had a 6GB drive inside. It also had a more familiar design modeled after portable CD players. But that made it bulkier than the competition; it weighed a shocking 14 ounces. Unsurprisingly, it also failed to usher MP3 players into the mainstream. It wasn’t until the introduction of the iPod in November 2001 that the golden age of portable media players truly took off. By 2007, roughly 20 percent of Americans owned a personal media player. Other companies, including Microsoft and Creative, tried to carve out space for themselves with Zune and Zen lines, respectively. But Apple’s iPod was the dominant force in the market, accounting for over 70 percent of media player sales. While 20 percent isn’t ubiquitous, the iPod and the digital music revolution certainly felt inescapable in the 2000s. Bands like Radiohead and Nine Inch Nails were experimenting with pay-what-you-want digital releases. Napster taught everyone the phrases “file sharing” and “peer-to-peer.” And Apple’s iconic ads combining silhouettes and white earbuds were everywhere. The personal media player’s spotlight was relatively short-lived. While Apple didn’t fully discontinue the iPod lineup until 2022, it retired the Classic model in 2014 and cut the Nano and Shuffle in 2017, leaving the iPod Touch — essentially an iPhone without the phone — as the last iPod standing. By 2011, the writing was on the wall as iPhone sales eclipsed iPod sales for the first time. The portable media player market shrank quickly as modern smartphones replaced flip phones and BlackBerrys, and music consumption moved away from purchasing CDs or digital downloads toward streaming. What was, at its peak, a $21.6 billion industry in 2008 had collapsed to just $613 million in 2012, according to research firm Mintel. How it’s going It’s difficult to get reliable numbers for the size of the digital audio player market these days. Some research firms lump all media players together, regardless of whether they’re audio or video, streaming or offline. Others that do track audio-specific players as a separate market segment can’t seem to agree. Some report that it’s a $180 million-plus industry on the rise. Others say it’s only a $1.2 million market and it’s shrinking. One thing is certain, though: Portable media players have become a very small niche. For most of the last 10 years, dedicated portable music players were primarily the realm of audiophiles. Companies like Sony and Astell & Kern have been steadily releasing high-end audio players that can sell for well north of $3,000. Sony’s NW-A306 is the only device offered by either company that even approaches a mainstream consumer price, at $399.99. These devices aren’t just more expensive, they’re more complicated than the iPods of yore. Wi-Fi and Bluetooth are a given. They feature large touchscreens and high-end digital audio converters. They also often run Android, opening them up to streaming apps like Spotify and Qobuz. Sony has fully embraced the iPod Touch model, giving its players full access to the Google Play store. The sky-high prices and embrace of apps has led many to reject these players. Instead, those looking for an offline listening experience free from notifications and algorithms have turned to the past. Vintage iPods still fetch hundreds of dollars on eBay. An entire cottage industry has cropped up around modding them — adding modern features like Bluetooth and USB-C, replacing the dying hard drives and batteries, or just customizing the appearance. What happens next As popular as the iPod was, the world’s supply of working used units will eventually run out. As they age, batteries will stop holding a charge and spinning drives will fail, and most people don’t want to open up a piece of delicate electronics or mess with a soldering iron. But the renewed interest in iPods is starting to drive up prices on other media players, and modders are now swapping new drives into Zunes and selling them for hundred of dollars on eBay. With Google searches for “MP3 player” nearly tripling since last year and The New York Times running trend pieces about the iPod resurgence, a number of companies and startups are trying to cash in. Chinese manufacturers have flooded AliExpress, Temu, and Amazon with a ton of dirt-cheap players and shameless iPod knockoffs. Wildly successful crowdfunding campaigns, like that of the AP30 Music Boy, show there is pent-up demand for retro portable music players. But most out there aren’t moving the needle much in terms of design or usability. Sleevenote is one startup that’s attempting to break the mold, but its success is far from guaranteed. It’s a startup from musician Tom Vek that embraces some modern conveniences like syncing over Wi-Fi and Bluetooth headphones, but skips on any extraneous features like streaming, apps, or games. It swaps scrolling text lists of artist names for a grid of album art. It’s highly visual, and attempts to re-create the experience of paging through a CD booklet. It also has limited integration with a host of digital music storefronts like Bandcamp, Subvert, Bleep, Qobuz, Amazon Music, and more. Vek has a promising-looking concept on its hands that actually approaches the portable media player in a fresh way. But the bulky Day One edition still has a lot of kinks to work out, including disappointing battery life. (I’ve been testing one for a couple of months now.) Plus, it’s currently sold out and the company doesn’t know when the next batch will be made available. There’s growing anti-streaming sentiment, and the slowtech trend doesn’t seem to be going anywhere anytime soon. But no obvious heir to the iPod throne has stepped in to fill the gap in the MP3 player market. It seems unlikely that the MP3 player will see a resurgence on the scale of vinyl or even CDs. In part because, for whatever convenience advantage an iPod might have over a limited edition LP, it lacks the collectibility factor. And that has been a major driver of the physical media resurgence, as evidenced by the fact that, while Gen Z and millennials might be buying up CDs in record numbers, half of them don’t own a CD player. By the way * Suzanne Vega is sometimes called the “mother of the MP3.” Karlheinz Brandenburg was working on audio compression technology at the Fraunhofer Society (FHG) in Germany and turned to Vega’s “Tom’s Diner” as his benchmark due to her “warm, human voice” that would be a challenge to encode. Thousands of miles away, James Johnston also turned to “Tom’s Diner” while working on audio compression at Bell Labs. Brandenburg and Johnston’s work ultimately led to the creation of MPEG-1 Audio Layer III standard, better known as MP3. * Kane Kramer is widely credited with inventing the first digital audio player in 1979, and successfully patented it in the UK in 1985, and the US in 1987. Many of its features, including an online music store, would eventually find their way into the iPod and iTunes. And Paul McCartney was an early financial backer, but his IXI never saw a commercial release. Kramer’s patents lapsed in 1988. While Apple eventually gave him credit for his invention, it was primarily a legal maneuver to undermine a company called Burst.com that sued Apple for patent infringement. Read this * Brandon Shaw, host of YouTube channel Digging the Greats, ditched streaming for an iPod two years ago and documented the experience over the course of several videos. * The New York Times looked at how younger generations were embracing old-school media formats, including the iPod, in an attempt to break free of the shackles of streaming. * The Verge crew shared their fond memories of the iPod when Apple officially put it out to pasture in 2022. * This visual history of the iPod charts its evolution from clunky brick to sleek icon of modern design.

articles.title: The iPad Mini is slightly cheaper again during Prime Day
articles.summary: October Prime Day is bringing down the price on the iPad Mini with the A17 Pro chip.
articles.body: Apple bumped up prices on several of its devices in June, and we haven’t seen a good discount on the iPad Mini since. Just ahead of Amazon’s October Prime Big Deals Days, however, both Wi-Fi only and cellular-connected models are $100 off. The Wi-Fi version with 128GB of storage is currently $499, the 256GB model is $599, and the cellular model with 128GB of storage is $649. This base configuration of this tablet often sold for around $400 throughout 2025, so we get it if $500 for a tablet from late 2024 is still too much. But it’s the best price since late June, and if there’s a new version coming out later this year, it might be significantly more expensive. [Product: iPad Mini (2024) | We reviewed this version of the iPad Mini when it launched in 2024, and while we appreciated the processor upgrade and Apple Intelligence features, it felt lacking in some of the quality-of-life improvements found in the larger iPads that launched around the same time. Read our Apple iPad Mini (2024) review.

articles.title: The AirPods Pro 3 are a fantastic deal at $179
articles.summary: For Amazon’s October Prime Day, you can snag a $70 discount on the Apple AirPods Pro 3 wireless earbuds.
articles.body: It’s been a while since we’ve seen a good discount on the Apple AirPods Pro 3, but like the latest iPad Mini and the M5 MacBook Airs, a great one is happening now for October Prime Day. You can snag a pair of the noise-canceling earbuds that include five ear tip sizes, live translation, and fantastic sound for $179 at Amazon (originally $249). I expect other retailers to offer a similar price in the coming days. This is the first time the price has gone below $190 since Prime Day in June. Since then, Apple launched the AirPods 5, and the most feature-complete version with a wireless charging case costs $149.99. Those are great if you prefer earbuds that don’t form a seal in your ears, but for everyone else, the AirPods Pro 3 are a much better value at just $30 more right now. articles.title: Alan Alda on fighting Parkinson's with laughter
articles.summary: Alan Alda, now 90, best-known for his role as "Hawkeye" Pierce on the classic TV series "M*A*S*H," talks about living with Parkinson's disease, which he refu...
articles.body:
Is it even possible to choose a favorite Alan Alda character? How about Senator Arnold Vinick on "The West Wing"? Or lawyer Jack Burroughs in "The Four Seasons"? And, of course, "Hawkeye" Pierce, the sarcastic Korean War combat surgeon, on "M*A*S*H"?

For his work on "M*A*S*H," which aired on CBS for 11 seasons beginning in 1972, Alda won five of his six Emmy Awards for acting, writing and directing.

"I have doctors coming up to me on the street all the time telling me that seeing me in the show made them want to become a doctor," Alda said. "Not a single one said it made them want to become an actor!"

Long before playing Pierce, Alda – now 90 – was on the other side of the stethoscope. As a seven-year-old he had polio, before there was a vaccine. "My father had just gotten a huge part in a movie, playing George Gershwin," he said. "And about a week after he started shooting, I got polio. And he and my mother had to administer the treatment, which was almost-scalding hot packs of wool on every limb. So, they were practically torturing their kid. I remember thinking it was hard on them."

As a boy, Alda studied his father Robert Alda's performances in vaudeville and burlesque, and also on Broadway, when Robert starred in the original cast of "Guys and Dolls." "I stood in the wings and watched that every Saturday," Alan said.

But Lady Luck dealt the family a difficult hand. His mother, Joan, a former beauty pageant winner, was complicated. "My mother was mentally ill, had schizophrenia and was paranoid," Alda said. "So sometimes the communication would be about the crack in the wall was where they had a camera taking pictures of us. I think that contributed a lot to tools I later had, trying to figure out what's real and what's not real. I had to pick one reality and try to stick with that. … It made me more observant. And I think it even helped – I'm just realizing this for the first time in this moment! – I think it made me a little more curious."

He's been especially curious about human connection, something he fostered on the set of "M*A*S*H." "We didn't go back to our dressing rooms between shots," he said. "It was just, like, an hour or two hours where they light the new set, we stayed in our chairs in a circle and made fun of one another and laughed. And that connection that we had, we carried with us onto the set."

Which had a huge impact on viewers. More than 100 million people watched the series' final episode. "They think 106. But I think it was probably more. Not that I'm greedy!" he laughed.

For years, Alda has been concerned that scientists and health care professionals often use technical language that's hard for the general public to understand. With that in mind, in 2009, New York's Stony Brook University founded the Alan Alda Center for Communicating Science . Back in 2013 , our own Tracy Smith watched Alda use methods from his own acting experience, including improvisation.

He said, "Improvisation really puts you in touch with the other person, and that's when I realized the value of connection."

Connecting is one of Alan Alda's superpowers. Since 2018, on his podcast "Clear+Vivid," he's been interviewing guests like Paul McCartney, Michael J. Fox, Noah Wyle, and recently, Joy Behar.

To Alda, connecting with people means being clear and honest, which is why he will openly discuss his Parkinson's disease. "I had a symptom, which at the time was not that well-known: Acting out your dreams," he said. "I had a dream that somebody was attacking me. And I picked up a sack of potatoes and threw it at 'em. What I was really doing was throwing a pillow at Arlene, my wife."

At the time he had no other symptoms: "I had no twitch, no tremor, no problems with my voice."

He was 79. A few years later, Alda decided to reveal the diagnosis. "I really think reality is my friend," he said. "I don't want to wish it away. I can't wish it away. I can't hope for a better future. I gotta accept what is."

There's currently no cure for the neurological disorder, but there are medications and other treatments. "I don't let Parkinson's define me," he said. "It's not who I am. It's just a hobby."

Which brings us to what Alda considers the importance of a sense of humor: "Very important, because the best way to deal with anything that's a little bit of a problem is to find out what's funny about it and laugh at it."

But what is funny about Parkinson's? "I'll be at the computer keyboard writing an email, and Dr. Parkinson is moving my hand all over the screen. I have the mouse, and he's eliminating things and he's deleting things that I need," Alda laughed. "Once in a while I get frustrated. But I find what makes me laugh about it, and then I go tell Arlene. Laughing first brought us together. We were invited to dinner at a friend's house. And Arlene was sitting at one end of the table, and I was sitting at the other end. And I noticed that she was laughing at my jokes. So already I was smitten. In March, we'll be married 70 years."

They have three daughters and eight grandchildren.

Alan Alda says he feels really good, even if Arlene has to help button his shirt in the morning, which he admitted he hated. "Of course, I feel that from time to time," Alda said. "I do hate it, but the only thing that's helpful is: what haven't I tried? And pretty soon, you get the feeling, 'If I keep looking for new ways to try this, I'll get a solution.' It's a puzzle. Will I be able eventually to put my socks on? The last time I put my socks on was a tremendous moment to celebrate!"

articles.title: This toolless modular lever-action wallet is the coolest I’ve stuck to my phone
articles.summary: The OhSnap Wallet 2 is a lever-action aluminum wallet with stackable modular parts, so a three card pocket wallet can transform into a seven card magnet one!
articles.body: This toolless modular lever-action wallet is the coolest I’ve stuck to my phone. Remember when I tested the ultra-thin and convenient OhSnap Snap Grip Stand and liked it so much I bought my own? Now, OhSnap has a magnetic lever-action card wallet that can stack with that stand. It’s the coolest wallet I’ve ever stuck to my phone. [Media: Pull the integrated springy lever, and your cards fan out. Want a thicker or thinner wallet? Press in the right place and it comes apart without tools, letting you swap in a 3, 5, or 7-card “core” that grips your cards so they don’t fall out. Want an ID card, work badge, elastic band for more cards, or a money clip on the end? You can change out the front or back magnetic plates for any of those. Or, change out both for ultra-thin aluminum covers if you don’t need the wallet to magnetically stick to your phone. You can see it in action in my Today I’m Toying With video embedded in this post (also on YouTube and on Instagram if you prefer). My favorite part is that the whole kit snaps together using a compliant mechanism — the plastic arms of the card-carrying core act like springs, pushing a little locking mechanism into the notches of each modular cover you add as you slide the parts together. Once your cards are inside, they keep the arms apart so it can’t open accidentally (unless you drop the entire wallet). It’s all very clever. [Image: With the ID card holder attached, and the core mounted to put the lever up instead of down. Even when I did drop the wallet (thanks for the suggestion, hugo!), it didn’t explode, typically. Usually, it just came apart slightly, though I did drop it hard on concrete one time and was able to make a small explosion: one half popped off, and two cards came out, but everything landed in a two-foot radius. The wallet has a big dent now. There are definitely some downsides. While OhSnap advertises the Wallet 2 as “impossibly thin,” it’s only truly surprisingly sleek in its thinnest 3-card variant, without the thicker and heavier MagSafe and MagStack (which lets you snap other magnets to it) plates attached. But the reason I’m not buying one is the price and weight. The 7-card version makes my phone feel too heavy, adding 127 grams, and while I happily made the 3-card my wallet for a few weeks, it’d cost me $61 on Kickstarter or $76 retail to get that with a double-magnet kit. OhSnap’s also charging more than I’d like ($35 for an ID cover or a money clip!) for extras. [Image: [Image: OhSnap didn’t get me this time. But I could see giving one as a present.

articles.title: Khatron Ke Khiladi 15 Winner: Avinash Mishra lifts the trophy; takes home Rs 20 lakh cash prize
articles.summary: After months of performing difficult and dangerous stunts, TV actor Avinash Mishra emerged as the winner of Khatron Ke Khiladi 15.
articles.body: After months of performing difficult and dangerous stunts, TV actor Avinash Mishra emerged as the winner of Khatron Ke Khiladi 15. The stunt-based reality show which took a break last year, returned after a highly anticipated two-year hiatus. Hosted by the action king Rohit Shetty, the season ended with Avinash Mishra being crowned the winner and Rithvik Dhanjani and Orhan Awatramani (Orry), emerging as the first and second runners-up, respectively. Season 15 was shot in the breathtaking terrains of Cape Town and introduced the high voltage ‘Champions vs. Challengers’ format. The Champions vs. Challengers saw the franchise veterans pitted against fresh contenders.The season featured scary machine stunts, the most discussed tough ‘Pain Auction’ task, Darr Ka Naya Daur which brought new challenges every week and kept viewers entertained.During the season, Avinash Mishra went from being a new contestant to one of the strongest performers. He proved that he was more than just a good-looking TV actor. His strong mindset and excellent stunt skills helped him stand out. He also gave several impressive performances during the show. As soon as host Rohit Shetty announced Avinash's name as the winner, the actor broke down in tears. Avinash told Rohit Shetty, "In the last 10 years, I've been nominated for several characters and have attended award functions, but this is the first time, I'm winning an award."After lifting the trophy, Avinash ran towards close friend Eisha Singh, who was sitting in the audience and hugged her tightly. The duo celebrated the occasion and were also seen getting teary-eyed.Avinash opens up about winner KKK 15Sharing his gratitude, Avinash Mishra said, “Winning Khatron Ke Khiladi feels special because I thought I signed up for the show with a point to prove, but along the way, the person I ended up proving it to, was myself. I have spent years being associated with television and, yes, with being the good-looking guy on screen. I enjoyed that journey, but I also knew there was so much more I wanted people to see in me. This show gave me the chance to put everything else aside and literally let my actions speak. Most of this journey was actually about the mind. You can prepare yourself physically, but when you are standing at the edge of something terrifying, there is no performance left – it is just you, your fear and the decision you make in that moment. I had to learn to tune out the noise, trust myself, and keep going. There were days when I surprised myself, and those are the moments I will cherish. And to win the show after everything I have discovered about myself here is the kind of ending I could only have hoped for. I came to Khatron Ke Khiladi wanting to test myself; I am leaving with a belief in myself that I didn’t have before. That, for me, is the biggest victory.”During the high-octane Team Week twist, he was appointed Team Captain and strategically steered his rookie squad entirely out of danger against a veteran-heavy team led by Rithvik Dhanjani. His fearless execution across dizzying heights and heavy machinery tasks earned him praise, and a highly coveted, signed custom Fear Jacket from Rohit Shetty. Avinash’s defining breakthrough arrived during a technically demanding, high-pressure underwater task, where he outperformed seasoned veteran Karan Wahi to claim a spot as the season’s very first Top 5 Finalist. His remarkable evolution culminated in an epic Grand Finale showdown, where Avinash conquered the ultimate helicopter-to-water stunt to emerge victoriously, taking home the coveted trophy, Rs 20 lakh cash prize and a brand-new car.Get the latest TV News, TV Shows and more. articles.title: California man arrested on charges of smuggling banned Nvidia chips to China; follows arrest of Super Micro Computer founder, may face 20 years in jail
articles.summary: A California man has been arrested over alleged chip smuggling. The 38-year-old owner of San Gabriel Valley-based Earthmade Computer Inc.
articles.body: A California man has been arrested over alleged chip smuggling. The 38-year-old owner of San Gabriel Valley-based Earthmade Computer Inc. is accused of smuggling more than $300 million worth of export-controlled computer servers containing US-manufactured graphics processing units (GPUs) to China. Prosecutors allege that Greg Lui, also known as “Yiu Kong Lui”, used false paperwork and routed the high-end servers through countries including Malaysia and Singapore before they were allegedly re-exported to China.The case follows US authorities' separate arrest of Super Micro Computer co-founder Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw in connection with an alleged scheme to divert Nvidia-powered AI servers to China. If convicted of all three charges, Lui could face up to 20 years in prison on the conspiracy and money laundering counts and up to 10 years on the smuggling count.California man accused of smuggling Nvidia chips to ChinaLui is charged with one count of conspiracy to violate the Export Control Reform Act and Export Administration Regulations, one count of outbound smuggling and one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering.“SI is the defining technology of the era,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “The National Security Division will protect the American advantage in the chips that power this technology, a product of our unparalleled innovation and hard work, from illegal diversion by our economic and military adversaries.”According to an indictment returned on Sept. 29, Lui allegedly used Earthmade to buy export-controlled items between 2023 and 2024 and send them to China without required US licences.Prosecutors allege that the equipment was first shipped to Malaysia and Singapore before being re-exported to China. They also allege that Lui provided false documentation to US manufacturers, misrepresenting the intended end users and destinations.From January to October 2024, Earthmade received more than $176 million from two Malaysia-based shipment companies as part of the alleged scheme.How the alleged scheme workedIn January 2024, Lui allegedly emailed a conspirator about a Malaysian transshipment company seeking 70 servers with export-restricted GPUs.Later that month, he allegedly ordered 27 servers from a US manufacturer for approximately $7.614 million. The servers were shipped from Los Angeles to Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, with documents identifying their GPUs as export-controlled equipment that could not be sent to China without a licence.In March 2024, a co-conspirator allegedly told a Malaysian government official that the 27 servers had been transshipped to a China-based buyer.“Protecting America’s national security means keeping our advanced Super Intelligence technology from being used to strengthen our adversaries’ military capabilities,” said First Assistant US Attorney Bill Essayli for the Central District of California. “This defendant allegedly used false paperwork and shipments through third countries to smuggle more than $300 million in export-controlled computer servers to China. We will aggressively prosecute those who put our national security at risk for profit.”FBI warns over advanced AI technology“The FBI’s investigation revealed that Lui allegedly sold the Chinese government hundreds of millions of dollars’ worth of American Super Intelligence technology, in clear violation of U.S. export control laws,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “Controlling the export of advanced SI technology is critical to safeguarding our national security and defending the homeland, and the FBI will keep fighting for America’s businesses and economic security. We’re grateful to our partners across the U.S. government and private sector for their assistance, and we’ll continue holding accountable anyone who violates U.S. export laws to enrich themselves and help our adversaries.”“Preventing the illegal export of controlled technology is critical to protecting our national security,” said Special Agent in Charge John E. Helsing of the Department of Defense Office of Inspector General Defense Criminal Investigative Service (DCIS) Western Field Office. “These technologies provide core advantages to U.S. forces, and ensuring they remain safeguarded prevents adversaries from exploiting them. Today’s action underscores our commitment to protecting advanced defense capabilities and enforcing the laws that keep them out of the hands of those who may threaten the United States.”Lui could face up to 20 years in prisonIf convicted of all charges, Lui could face a maximum of 20 years in prison on the conspiracy count, 20 years on the money laundering count and 10 years on the smuggling count.The Bureau of Industry and Security, Defense Criminal Investigative Service and FBI are investigating the case. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Colin S. Scott and Joseph S. Guzman, along with Trial Attorney Eli Ross, are prosecuting the case.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: India needs its own AI safety framework, not a copy of US pact: Industry experts
articles.summary: India should build its own artificial intelligence (AI) safety framework suited to its languages, scale, and application-led AI ecosystem rather than
articles.body: India should build its own artificial intelligence (AI) safety framework suited to its languages, scale, and application-led AI ecosystem rather than replicate a voluntary pact signed by US President Donald Trump and top technology firms last week, industry experts said.They also called for a commitment that brings together all stakeholders and tackles risks such as deepfakes and cyberattacks, even as they differed on whether voluntary measures alone would be enough.The comments came after the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, a voluntary AI safety pact signed on September 29 by Trump and top executives from Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Nvidia and Elon Musk's xAI.Under the accord, the companies committed to internal controls to monitor their AI models, dedicated oversight teams, independent external audits and board-level oversight. They also agreed to meet regularly to set safety standards.Nasscom Chairman and Fractal Group CEO Srikanth Velamakanni said India should not simply replicate the US. Instead, it should use a domestic commitment as a building block towards a global understanding of AI safety."As models become more capable and agentic, we are giving them greater access to systems and greater autonomy to make decisions. AI safety must be strengthened considerably and must stay ahead of capability to prevent catastrophic risks," Velamakanni said.He noted that the US accord is largely a push for self-policing by frontier AI companies. The European Union, by contrast, has taken a binding, risk-based approach, while China follows a state-directed control model.India, the Nasscom Chairman said, could use its role in the Global Partnership on AI (GPAI) and the momentum from hosting the AI Impact Summit in February to prevent worst-case outcomes, without citizens of India and the Global South being denied access to frontier models."India doesn't need to copy the US model, but it can take inspiration from it and expedite efforts to build a trusted AI ecosystem," said Soumen Mandal, Principal Analyst at Counterpoint Research.He added that such a commitment should cover testing AI systems before deployment, independent audits, reporting serious problems, and naming people responsible for AI-related risks.Amit Khanna, Partner and Automation Ecosystem Leader at Grant Thornton Bharat, said any commitment should be suited to Indian market conditions.He noted that India's focus is on building AI applications rather than major foundational models."An industry commitment in India should ensure AI works reliably across vernacular languages and unique cultural contexts and should not exploit AI knowledge asymmetry in the population," Khanna said.Ganesh Gopalan, co-founder and CEO of Gnani.ai, said any framework must ensure a level playing field.Global frontier models should be subject to the same rules as Indian ones, he said, since Indian AI companies compete with global firms for the same customers.The experts differed on whether self-regulation would be enough."Voluntary, self-regulatory approaches are necessary but woefully insufficient," Velamakanni said."Pharmaceuticals and aviation are great examples of industries where strong, technically competent regulators have strengthened safety and public trust without stopping innovation."He said India needs binding rules on transparency, incident reporting, and accountability when serious harm occurs.The IndiaAI Safety Institute should be strengthened to test newly released models, but without creating a bottleneck by requiring pre-release certification of every model, he added.Mandal backed a hybrid approach. Mandatory rules would apply to potential harms in defence, healthcare, banking, and government use cases, while voluntary standards would cover fast-moving technical areas where regulators may lack technical expertise."This type of hybrid approach will provide flexibility to AI companies instead of restricting every line of code while ensuring safety and privacy are not compromised," he said.Khanna also called for a hybrid "techno-legal" approach. It would pair a strong voluntary layer with binding mandates, such as the provisions on synthetically generated information in the IT Amendment Rules, 2026.He said voluntary compliance alone leaves significant gaps, particularly in civil rights and public safety.Gopalan, however, favoured self-regulation."Voluntary self-regulation is key given the technology is new. Having mandatory regulation can stifle competition and lead to concerns about a few companies getting preferential treatment."India needs more than 100 frontier AI lab companies, and that's the need of the hour to prevent India from being colonised, which is inevitable if we lag behind in the AI race," Gopalan said.The Indian government is in the process of bringing in its own AI regulation.Earlier this year, IT Secretary S Krishnan noted that while existing legal provisions have so far been adequate in addressing initial concerns on issues like deepfakes and AI-generated synthetic content, an "additional regulation or law may be needed"."It is a conversation which has commenced, and my minister (IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw) and I have both been on record earlier that we will look at AI regulation when the time is right, and it appears that the time is getting right, and we will start looking at it," he had said.Vaishnaw had also said that the current information technology law was framed much before the rapid emergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and that a new legal framework may be required to deal with the changing landscape.The industry agrees that any pact should go beyond AI companies."This cannot be an agreement among AI companies alone," Velamakanni said.He said the government, frontier model developers, large deployers, including enterprises and public agencies, academia, and independent safety researchers should all have defined roles. Workers, users, and civil society should have formal channels to report harms.He added that safety evaluations of frontier models should be carried out by independent, expert institutions and published, with narrow exceptions where disclosure itself creates a security risk.Mandal said the agreement should bring together the entire AI ecosystem, from AI companies and their business users to regulators, universities, researchers, workers, and users.Khanna argued that it should include government and public sector bodies, which would be major users of AI, as well as civil society, worker unions, and technology companies.Meanwhile, Gopalan called for broader self-regulation across the AI ecosystem to ensure impartial access to limited compute resources.Velamakanni said the top concern must be preventing catastrophic and systemic harms.He listed large-scale cyberattacks, electoral interference, biological or chemical weapons, attacks on critical infrastructure, and loss of control over highly autonomous systems. Individual harms such as deepfakes, fraud, impersonation, privacy breaches, and self-harm come next."Autonomy must lag behind assurance to provide a margin of safety. As AI systems gain the ability to act in the world (use tools, move money, change systems, make consequential decisions), the evidence that they are safe and controllable must grow faster than the autonomy we give them," he said.Gopalan said that given India's large population and democratic framework, the bigger concerns are deepfakes and cyberattacks targeting financial institutions.Khanna also named deepfakes as the top immediate priority.He described misinformation, deepfakes, and political manipulation as "existential threats to India's social fabric".He said rules on liability when AI systems fail, such as misdiagnosing a patient or wrongly denying welfare benefits, remain a critical gap.Mandal placed independent audits first, followed by accountability, data protection, deepfakes, and job impact."Without independent testing and audits, the system will not be complete, as companies may sometimes overlook AI-related concerns," he said.You use AI every day. articles.body: Google has waited until the day its new Googlebook laptops hit the market to admit that Intel-based models may have issues running some Android apps. Before now, Google has emphasized that the Android-based Googlebooks give owners access to the “entire Play Store library” of apps, along with some clever interactions with Android phones and tablets. Today, in a statement to Android Authority, it admitted that while every app is available, some may not offer smooth performance on every Googlebook. > The vast majority of Android apps run smoothly across both Intel and Qualcomm Googlebooks right out of the box. Because many Android apps were originally designed for Arm chips, a small handful of complex apps or games need some developer tuning to run their best on Intel-based platforms. We’re working hand-in-hand with app developers, Intel, and Qualcomm to continuously optimize performance and expand compatibility across the entire portfolio. Google hasn’t said how many apps will have performance issues, or named any specific apps that may have problems. Of the five Googlebook laptops that have gone on sale today, three — models from Acer, Asus, and Lenovo — run on x86 Intel chips. The Dell and HP models instead run on Qualcomm’s Arm-based Snapdragon processors, and so should have greater compatibility with every Android app. We’ll be testing all five Googlebooks across the Verge team, and will report back on specific issues we find.

articles.title: New TV shows to watch this week: Tune in to 'Cupertino' on CBS, stream 'Carrie' on Prime Video and revisit 'The Haunting of Hill House' on Netflix
articles.summary: The new TV shows worth watching — from the HBO divorce drama "War" to Netflix's "East of Eden" adaptation and a seaside mystery starring Josh Hartnett.
articles.body:
Hey, TV watchers! TV critic Michel Ghanem here. Every two weeks, I highlight the shows worth your TV time for Trust Me, I Watch Everything . Whether you prefer sticking to cable, catching the latest on streaming or digging up a hidden gem that slipped through the cracks, I try to curate something for everyone.

Happy spooky month ! If you're a fan of horror, there's lots ahead, whether that's American Horror Story on FX or a new take on Stephen King's iconic Carrie on Prime Video. Otherwise, consider tuning in to two juicy legal dramas: Cupertino on CBS and War on HBO, or stream Netflix's highly anticipated East of Eden adaptation. Finally, it's the perfect time to revisit Mike Flanagan's best miniseries, The Haunting of Hill House , also on Netflix. Let's jump into this week's recommendations.

Why you should watch it: Remember The Good Wife ? The creators of the Emmy-winning drama return with another 20-episode legal drama for CBS. There are few showrunners who are able to craft such engaging, dynamic courtroom scenes as Michelle and Robert King. Cupertino , their latest, is no exception.

This time around, we're not in Chicago but in the depths of Silicon Valley. The series begins when attorneys Michael Price (Mike Colter, who also appeared in The Good Wife , The Good Fight and Evil ) and Olivia Siffre (Rachel Keller) are both fired from the same tech startup. They decide to start a new law firm together, at first to take down their ex-employer, but eventually drawing the attention of other victims of Big Tech who need legal representation.

While the show embraces a case-of-the-week structure, it's also about their new firm getting off the ground, gaining investors and catching the eye of billionaires with deep pockets. Michael and Olivia barely have any money or much of a reputation to get started, but they have the power of the law on their side. It's reminiscent of some of the best David-vs.-Goliath tensions in The Good Wife .

There is also some pretty interesting character development right off the bat: Michael is trying to get out from under the shadow of his wealthy and successful lawyer father, Bayard (Joe Morton), and Olivia is timid and religious, which she's ultimately able to wield to her advantage against unsuspecting clients. You can also look forward to some great recurring appearances by Busy Philipps and Renée Elise Goldsberry.

To Cupertino 's credit, the individual cases are extremely entertaining to follow, which isn't always the case in legal procedurals. Not only are they topical — AI comes up a lot, naturally — but they're approached with curiosity and skepticism, enough to make our protagonists question their own preconceived biases.

In this way, Cupertino is the best of both worlds between The Good Wife and Evil , another show by the Kings that tackled religion rather than technology. This may be one of the best new broadcast shows in recent memory, and thank goodness we have an old-fashioned 20-episode season that will see us until summer.

How to watch: New episodes of Cupertino air every Thursday at 10 p.m. ET on CBS and stream on Paramount+ beginning Oct. 8.

Why you should watch it : Is divorce a battlefield? War seems to think so. In HBO's latest juicy drama, which was created by George Kay ( Hijack , Lupin ), two halves of a married couple take their legal teams to battle in a messy divorce with twists and turns.

It all kicks off when Carla Duval (Sienna Miller), a well-known actor based in London, suspects her husband of 10 years, Morgan Henderson (Dominic West), of having extramarital affairs. To get to the bottom of it, she sends a woman to seduce him after a big night in which he receives an award for Zephyr, the social media platform he created. Unfortunately, it works; he sleeps with the woman, and the divorce kicks off from there.

This is less a drama about a marriage collapsing or even how the public picks apart high-profile divorce cases, and much more a look into the legal process of it all. We spend a lot of time with two legal teams: Taylor & Byrne, led by married couple Nicholas Taylor (James McArdle) and Serena Byrne (Phoebe Fox), who are representing Carla, and Morgan's Cathcarts firm, led by Beatrice Ubosi (Nina Sosanya) and St. John Smallwood (Pip Torrens). This creates a large ensemble cast that is fun to follow over eight episodes as the proceedings pick up steam and we head for the inevitable court case.

A wild card in the series is Johnny Warren (Archie Renaux), a young law school graduate desperate to escape his job waiting tables and succeed in the field. His desire to do this at any cost places him in some precarious (and yet fairly predictable) circumstances.

At times, War could use more punch — debates on how to split up assets can be a bit dry to watch — but things get twistier from the fifth episode onward, and we spend a lot of the season with the tension that the other shoe will drop eventually. It helps that War is extremely sleek — well-shot, costumed and produced overall, with both Miller and West delivering solid performances.

How to watch: New episodes of War air on Thursdays at 9 p.m. ET on HBO and stream on HBO Max .

American Horror Story : The 13th season of Ryan Murphy's horror anthology is bringing back many of its original actors, including Kathy Bates, Jessica Lange and Angela Bassett, for an all-star edition. The show is pulling lore from its first few seasons in particular, so it's probably not the most beginner-friendly season to dive into. But if you love this campy, chaotic universe, this is one to watch for the spooky season. — New episodes air on Thursday at 9 p.m. ET on FX and stream simultaneously on Hulu .

Tip Toe: A psychological thriller created by Russell T. Davies that aired to polarizing opinions in the U.K. has arrived stateside. It stars The Traitors host Alan Cumming as Leo Struthers, a bar owner in Manchester who develops an antagonistic relationship with his electrician neighbor, Clive (David Morrissey), while anti-LGBTQ rhetoric rises on social media. If you were a fan of Davies's previous politically driven shows like Years and Years or It's a Sin , you'll want to tune in. — New episodes air Fridays at 9:05 p.m. ET on Starz .

Why you should watch it: We all know the Stephen King story of Carrie, the high school student with mysterious powers who was relentlessly bullied in high school, only to be maliciously crowned prom queen and covered in pig's blood during her coronation. There have been many adaptations since the 1974 novel, most notably the 1976 film starring Sissy Spacek. Now comes the latest iteration of Carrie — and it's an exciting new take.

For one, this is the first time this story is being adapted into a television series, stretched over eight episodes. It's also helmed by Mike Flanagan, a veteran of television horror who once produced a season of television for Netflix every year ( The Haunting of Hill House and Midnight Mass are two of his best). Crucially, this version of the story takes place in the present day rather than the '70s, meaning the bullying Carrie (Summer H. Howell) experiences follows her in person and virtually.

If you're already familiar with this tale, there are plenty of scenes that might feel familiar, like Carrie getting her period or Miss Desjardin (Amber Midthunder) punishing her gym class students for picking on Carrie by making them run drills. The role of Carrie's feverishly religious mother, Margaret (Samantha Sloyan), is expanded, and more details are inserted to explain why Carrie is forced to start attending public school after a childhood of homeschooling.

The season's structure is also more reminiscent of the novel, offering a Greek chorus of sorts by featuring police interviews in the aftermath and differing perspectives (I like to think of it as the Big Little Lies narrative device).

Flanagan has a three-season plan for Carrie , and you can see the ways in which he sprinkles in a story that reaches beyond Carrie's high school experience (i.e., introducing other individuals with supernatural abilities). For me, Carrie strikes the perfect balance of clarifying gaps in the original story while being entertaining and a little spooky — absolutely worth the binge this Halloween season.

How to watch: All eight episodes of Carrie will stream on Wednesday, Oct. 7, on Prime Video .

East of Eden : Zoe Kazan's highly anticipated miniseries adaptation of East of Eden has arrived, and it is sumptuous and epic, even when it's dark and miserable. The series stars Florence Pugh as Cathy Ames alongside Christopher Abbott and Mike Faist. This one is an immediate awards contender and one of Netflix's biggest swings in a while, with gorgeous cinematography and heart-wrenching performances. Not a series you'll want to miss. — All seven episodes are streaming on Netflix .

Below : If you liked Widow's Bay , you're in luck: Another spooky seaside horror mystery has arrived. In Below , we're in a small town in Newfoundland, Canada, where fisherman Calvin Penney (Josh Hartnett) encounters a mysterious sea creature. The cast is rounded out by Mackenzie Davis and Charlie Heaton. Expect many frights. — All six episodes will stream on Netflix on Thursday, Oct. 8.

Avatar: Seven Havens: The next series in the animated universe of Avatar: The Last Airbender is finally upon us. Set 225 years after the events of The Legend of Korra , in which the world has been transformed by a cataclysmic apocalyptic event , we follow Avatar Pavi (Saheli Khan), an earthbender living in the city of Ellora, who reunites with her long-lost sister Nisha (Aishu Devan). The Avatar world is one of the richest fictional universes on television, and it's about time creators Michael Dante DiMartino and Bryan Konietzko continue to grow its lore. — Three new episodes are streaming every Friday starting Oct. 9 on Paramount+ .

Why you should watch it: If you have an interest in horror but haven't yet dipped into the works of filmmaker Mike Flanagan, The Haunting of Hill House is where you should start. It's not a series you'll be able to get out of your head anytime soon.

Hill House routinely ranks at the top of critic lists for the best shows on Netflix, and it's easy to see why. Loosely adapted from Shirley Jackson's chilling 1959 novel of the same name, the series follows the Crain family in 1992 as they move into an old mansion with the hope of flipping it for profit. Over the course of the renovations, the family is exposed to paranormal activity that intensifies until it finally drives them from the mansion.

Twenty-six years later, the five Crain siblings are still processing what happened to them as kids. Steven (Michiel Huisman) has made a career out of publishing semi-autobiographical novels about ghosts; Shirley (Elizabeth Reaser) runs a mortuary with her husband; Luke (Oliver Jackson-Cohen) hasn't been able to move past his childhood experiences and leans on a heroin addiction to cope; Theo (Kate Siegel) is a child psychologist; and Nell (Victoria Pedretti) is found dead at the beginning of the series, bringing the siblings together to mourn her loss.

We flash back and forth between the 1992 and 2018 timelines as the siblings are essentially forced to revisit the paranormal trauma they've each buried or suppressed in their own way. The jump scares in both timelines are bone-chillingly good, and there is a twist about what happened to Nell in the fifth episode that is one of the best in recent television memory — I still get shivers thinking about it.

There's a reason why Hill House has endured as one of Netflix's best. It is extremely evocative, gorgeously crafted and performed, and was absolutely deserving of Emmy nominations it never received. I can't think of a better time to watch it than October.

How to watch: All 10 episodes of The Haunting of Hill House are streaming on Netflix.

That's it for this edition, but there'll always be more TV to watch. I'll be back on Oct. 19 with new recommendations.

Think there's something missing that deserves my TV time? Let me know what else I should have on my radar in the comments below!

articles.title: TCL’s paperlike OLED phone made me more excited for the iPhone Duo
articles.summary: More phones should have matte displays like the TCL P80 Ultra Nxtpaper.
articles.body: I’ve spent most of the last couple weeks using an otherwise unexceptional midrange Android phone with one amazing feature: a matte OLED display. That screen is by far the best thing about the TCL P80 Ultra, and weirdly, it’s made me more excited for the iPhone Duo and its matte inner display. 2023’s TCL Nxtpaper 40 first brought matte displays to the company’s phones, after they appeared on tablets in 2021. Nxtpaper is more than a simple matte finish on a panel: it also includes a paperlike feel and low-power, monochrome modes that create a reasonable facsimile of an E Ink screen. But the matte effect has always been the biggest draw for me. The P80 Ultra’s screen is special because it’s the first to combine the Nxtpaper tech with an OLED panel. That means it’s the best-looking Nxtpaper screen yet, with deeper blacks, better contrast, and richer colors. Previous models have felt a little visually compromised; this one doesn’t. It also finally enables an always-on display. Always-on displays have been the norm on Android for years, and the fact that TCL’s Nxtpaper phones didn’t have them was a dealbreaker for many. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: I’ve used a couple of Nxtpaper phones over the last few years, but usually found the tradeoffs — both across the specs and in the screen itself — never quite made sense. In some respects, that’s still true for the P80 Ultra, which I can’t entirely recommend as a phone in its own right. Performance has been sluggish and stuttering, and while the triple rear camera has decent enough specs on paper, photo quality is distinctly average. The difference now is that the display feels like all upside. As an OLED, it’s bright and beautiful, with enough color and contrast to suit both scrolling and streaming. But the matte finish keeps it comfortable to look at, even at cranked up brightness or in a dimly lit room, with less flicker and blue light than most other displays. Nxtpaper’s anti-glare effect actually makes this a really excellent phone to use in brighter environments. It looked great under the bright lights of TCL’s IFA tradeshow booth, no mean feat. And the viewing angles are truly excellent, with good visibility even when the phone is almost entirely side-on. That’s without touching on the texture, which is smooth and satiny, so your finger sticks just a little less when swiping. It’s a small thing, but a welcome one. [Image: [Image: Because this is a Nxtpaper phone, it goes a little further. A dedicated toggle on the phone’s side triggers one of two more substantial overhauls to the display. Paper Mode washes out the display’s color — or can go fully monochromatic if you prefer — to make it even easier on your eyes, with the option to exclude individual apps so they run as usual. Streaming apps and games are exempted by default. Max Ink Mode is more drastic: it’s strictly monochrome and removes access to most apps and OS features, giving you a power-efficient mode with minimal distractions, turning the P80 Ultra into something between an e-reader and a dumb phone. Although most other phones are limited to aftermarket matte screen protectors to get anything like the same effect, TCL isn’t the only manufacturer making hardware with a matte display. Huawei has made a string of tablets with what it calls PaperMatte panels, and Lenovo and Xiaomi offer similar screens on select models. Matte screens underpin the painterly effect of Samsung’s Frame TVs (and imitations from rivals including TCL). And then, of course, there’s Apple’s nano-texture glass. [Image: The iPhone Duo’s OLED inner screen has a matte coating too. Apple’s offered this coating as an option on iPad Pro models since 2024, selling it on the basis that its paperlike qualities are beneficial to anyone using the iPad Pro as a drawing device. It’s now appearing on a phone for the first time in the iPhone Duo, with Apple relying on the anti-glare effect to minimize the visibility of the foldable panel’s crease. I haven’t had the chance to try the Duo yet, but using the P80 Ultra has made me more excited to. Pairing a matte effect with the Duo’s large inner screen sounds great, and it’s one of the few elements of the Duo that no Android foldable can currently match. My only hesitation is that Apple didn’t make the outer panel matte too — an odd choice given how much it’s emphasized the seamless switch between the two screens — so I worry the transition might be jarring. Given the book-style form factor, Apple will also be missing a trick if it doesn’t create its own e-reader-inspired mode for the Duo to match TCL’s, though the existing grayscale mode might be a decent imitation. Perhaps what’s most exciting about an iPhone adopting a matte panel is that within the year we’ll probably see Android brands imitate it, something TCL wasn’t able to inspire. We’ve already seen the Duo’s squat form factor appear in handsets from Samsung, Xiaomi, and Huawei, with Motorola teasing its own too. The Duo’s matte layer hasn’t yet sparked its own imitators, but I suspect it’s only a matter of time, especially if it helps hide foldable creases. Not every phone needs to be matte, but I would love more of them to give me the option. Hopefully Apple’s industry influence grants me my wish.

articles.title: Huge fire breaks out near ‘Pati Patni Aur Panga 2’ and Hustle 5 sets in Mumbai's Film City; No casualties reported
articles.summary: Pati Patni Aur Panga, which is set to return with its second season, faced a tense situation after a fire broke out at Mumbai’s Film City on Monday,
articles.body: Pati Patni Aur Panga, which is set to return with its second season, faced a tense situation after a fire broke out at Mumbai’s Film City on Monday, October 5. The fire reportedly started outside the sets of Pati Patni Aur Panga 2 and MTV Hustle 5. Videos from the spot circulating on social media show huge flames and thick black smoke rising from the area. Both teams are reportedly safe after the incident; no one was injured. They also assured that everyone is safe.Sources close to the show Pati Patni Aur Panga, confirmed that fire erupted outside the sets. The team shared, "Fire took place today but it did not happen on the sets, it was outside the sets. There has been no casualty as nobody was shooting on the set of Pati Patni Aur Panga. There was no shoot planned for today."The makers of MTV Hustle 5 shared a statement with TOI and confirmed the incident. However, the team assured that everyone is safe."Everyone is safe. The fire broke out outside the Pati Patni Aur Panga set, next to the Hustle 5 set. We were shooting for the Hustle 5 Grand Finale when the fire was spotted during the papping. Everyone was alerted and managed to evacuate in time. No one was harmed and there were no casualties," said the team.In a statement to Hindustan Times, The Hustle 5 team confirmed that the grand finale shoot was in progress when the fire broke out. All the artists were present on the sets at the time. Badshah, EPR, MC Square, Paradox and Agsy are among the artists associated with the season. The team shared “All the artists were there when the fire suddenly broke out. As of now, there are no casualties and everyone is safe."Actor and The Hustle 5 host Samarth Jurel also shared a video from the sets and informed that a massive first broke out on the sets of the rapping reality show. However, he later deleted the video.Quoting a source from The Hustle 5 sets, Hindustan Times shared that the incident took place while singer Nikita Gandhi was being photographed by the paparazzi at the location. The source informed the publication, “Nikita Gandhi’s paparazzi spotting was happening when this unfortunate incident took place."The cause of the fire is not yet known. The Hustle 5 team also shared that everyone has left the sets for now. The team shared, “As soon as the fire broke out, everyone left the sets. We still don’t know what caused the fire, but thankfully, everyone is safe."Get the latest TV News, TV Shows and more. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Nvidia’s Shield TV Pro just got a $100 price hike
articles.summary: The ongoing memory shortage has come for Nvidia’s seven year old Shield TV Pro streaming box which jumps from $200 to $300 this month.
articles.body: Nvidia’s Shield TV streaming boxes are the latest victims of the memory shortage that has seen prices increase dramatically for everything from digital cameras to game consoles. When the Shield TV Pro launched nearly seven years ago with an upgraded Tegra X1+ processor, 3GB of RAM, and 16GB of storage, it sold for $199.99. But starting on October 2nd Nvidia increased its price by $100 to $299.99 as a result of the increased cost of components, according to Ars Technica. When the Pro model was first announced in 2019 Nvidia also debuted an updated entry-level version of the Shield TV with the same processor but 2GB of RAM and 8GB of storage priced at $149.99. Unfortunately, it will no longer be an option for those now looking for a cheaper alternative to the Shield TV Pro. Nvidia has stopped production of the standard Shield TV model and moving forward it’s focusing its efforts on only manufacturing the Pro option, according to Gizmodo. High demand for Nvidia’s other hardware including GPUs and AI chips has been a major contributor to the dramatic price increases of components and devices over the past few years. So while this price increase may reduce demand for the Shield TV Pro while competing streaming boxes like the $149 Google TV Streamer are much cheaper (even after recent price hikes), it won’t affect Nvidia’s value as the company continues to dominate the AI race.
